metaTitle: Peppermint Oil for Mice: What the Evidence Says
metaDescription: Peppermint oil is not a proven way to clear mice from a home. See what the research and federal guidance say, the risk to cats and what to do instead.
h1: Peppermint Oil for Mice: Does It Work, and Is It Safe for Pets?
dek: What the research on plant oils and rodents found, what an EPA-exempt peppermint label does and does not promise, the danger to cats, and the steps that do get mice out.
excerpt: Peppermint oil is a popular mouse remedy, but a research review found plant-compound repellents inconsistent, and CDC guidance relies on sealing holes. Pet risks included.

quickAnswer.lead: **Peppermint oil is not a proven way to drive mice out of a home.** A [2016 review of 54 publications on plant compounds and rodents](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27613544/) found the strongest laboratory effects came from essential oils and terpenoids, but success was inconsistent across laboratory, enclosure and field studies. The CDC and University of California guidance cited here relies on sealing, sanitation and trapping, and Pet Poison Helpline lists peppermint oil among oils known to poison cats.
bullets: A 2016 systematic review screened 54 publications and found the strongest laboratory effects in essential oils and terpenoids, with inconsistent success across laboratory, enclosure and field studies.
CDC says a mouse can fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch (6 mm), which no smell can close.
Peppermint oil is on the federal list of ingredients eligible for EPA's minimum-risk exemption, and EPA says it does not review exempted products.
UC IPM says mice quickly become accustomed to regularly repeated sounds, but none of the sources cited here tests whether they do the same with a scent.
Pet Poison Helpline lists peppermint oil among the essential oils known to cause poisoning in cats, and says cats and birds are at the greatest risk from essential oils.
UC IPM calls exclusion, meaning sealing the building, the most successful and permanent form of house mouse control.

body.text: Does peppermint oil keep mice away?

Not reliably, and none of the sources cited on this page shows that peppermint oil clears mice out of a home. [A 2016 systematic review of plant compounds as rodent repellents](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27613544/) screened 54 publications in which plant compounds or plants were tested for their effect on rodent behavior or metabolism. Its authors report that essential oils and terpenoids produced the strongest effects across species in laboratory experiments, and that success was inconsistent across laboratory, enclosure and field studies. Peppermint oil is an essential oil, so the laboratory result explains why the idea is plausible, and the inconsistency explains why it is a risky thing to rely on.

The government and university guidance cited here leaves scents out. [CDC's guidance on sealing up](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/seal-up.html) is about closing holes and cutting off food and water, and the page does not mention repellents. [The University of California's house mouse note](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7483.html) calls exclusion the most successful and permanent form of house mouse control and does not mention peppermint oil. Neither source calls scents useless. They simply build a control plan without them.

The rest of this page covers where the idea comes from, what the research can and cannot support, what a peppermint product label is allowed to say, the risk to cats and other pets, and where a scent could fit once the real work is done. For the full sequence of sealing, trapping and cleaning up, see [the complete mouse control reference](/learn/mice). For how peppermint compares with ultrasonic devices, predator scents and other deterrents, see [the overview of mouse repellents by type](/blog/mice-repellent).
Where does the idea that peppermint oil repels mice come from?

It comes from a theory that sounds sensible: a smell strong enough to bother a mouse should make it avoid the place. Peppermint oil is easy to buy, has an intense minty smell to people, and appears on many lists of home remedies for pests, including the one weighed in [the guide to which smells mice are said to hate](/blog/what-smells-do-mice-hate).

The theory has some scientific footing. In the 2016 review, essential oil and terpenoid compounds showed the strongest effects across species in laboratory experiments, so researchers have reason to keep studying them. The authors recommend systematic screening of plant compounds across several species, especially essential oils and terpenoids. That is a call for more research, not a finding that a household remedy works.

Two other things may help keep the idea alive. Peppermint oil is on the federal list of ingredients that can go into an exempt, minimum-risk pesticide product, and EPA says it does not review exempted products, so no federal review checks whether a given product works. And signs of mice can come and go for reasons that have nothing to do with any product, so a quiet week after using one is easy to read as proof. Plant-based products as a whole, and what they can and cannot do, are examined in [the guide to natural pest control](/blog/natural-pest-control).
What does the research on peppermint oil and mice show?

It shows that plant compounds can change what rodents do in laboratory experiments, and that success has been inconsistent across laboratory, enclosure and field studies. The 2016 review's abstract ties that inconsistency to the small number of plant-based rodent repellents that are currently registered. Its strongest result is for a group of compounds, essential oils and terpenoids, and the abstract does not name peppermint, so it is not a result for the peppermint oil sold in a bottle.

A laboratory test can show that a mouse in a cage spent less time near a treated food dish. Whether a mouse that already lives in your wall, with a nest and a known food source close by, will abandon them is a different question, and it is the one a homeowner needs answered. That gap between a cage and a house is reasoning on this page's part, not a statement from the review, but it is consistent with the review's finding of inconsistent success across study types.

body.text: Read the table for what it leaves out as well as what it says. A guidance page that does not mention peppermint offers no evidence either way, and silence is all the CDC and UC IPM pages offer on this question. The only research evidence on this page is the 2016 review, and it speaks about plant compounds as a group.
What would convincing evidence look like?

A convincing test would put a peppermint product in occupied homes, compare them with similar homes left untreated, and count mice by an objective measure such as trap catch or droppings over several weeks, with the results reported by researchers who do not sell the product. None of the sources cited on this page gives the result of a test of that kind for peppermint oil, which is why this page cannot offer a dose, a placement distance or a replacement interval.
Is peppermint oil an EPA-approved mouse repellent?

Not in the usual sense: peppermint oil is an ingredient allowed under EPA's minimum-risk exemption, and EPA does not review the products sold under it. Under [EPA's conditions for minimum risk pesticides](https://www.epa.gov/minimum-risk-pesticides/conditions-minimum-risk-pesticides), a product that meets six conditions does not need to be registered with EPA. The first condition is that its active ingredients, meaning the ingredients that kill, repel or mitigate the pests named on the label, must be ones listed in the federal regulation at 40 CFR 152.25(f)(1). That list includes both peppermint and peppermint oil, along with other plant products that turn up in home pest advice, such as cinnamon oil, clove oil, rosemary oil, cedarwood oil, garlic and castor oil.

What it means for a peppermint product

Only ingredients listed in 40 CFR 152.25(f)(1)
Peppermint oil is on the list, so it can be the active ingredient.

The carrier or filler is restricted too.

All ingredients listed by name, with each active ingredient's percentage by weight
The label should tell you how much peppermint oil the product contains.

No claim to control or mitigate organisms that pose a threat to human health, or insects or rodents carrying specific diseases
EPA's own example is that a label may say a product controls ticks, but not that it controls ticks that carry Lyme disease. Rodents carrying specific diseases fall under the same condition.
Company identity
The name of the producer, or of the company the product was made for, and its contact information displayed prominently
You can see who is responsible for the product.
No false or misleading statements
Nothing false or misleading about the product's composition or effectiveness, and nothing implying that a federal agency recommends or endorses it
EPA's example of a misleading statement is a label saying the product is recommended by EPA as safe and exempt, because EPA does not review exempted products.
body.caption: Source: EPA's conditions page, which points to 40 CFR 152.25(f). States may also require registration under their own laws.

body.text: None of this is a ruling on whether peppermint works. The exemption is a rule about ingredients and labels. Because EPA does not review exempted products, it has not evaluated whether any exempt peppermint repellent keeps mice away. EPA's page also says states may require registration under state law, so a product sold in one state can face extra rules in another.

In practice, you cannot read federal approval into a peppermint product's packaging. Look for the ingredient list, the percentage of peppermint oil and the producer's contact details that the conditions require, and treat any wording that suggests government endorsement as a red flag. One widely searched brand of scent pouch is examined in [the explainer on what Vamoose pouches contain and claim](/blog/vamoose-for-mice).
How do people use peppermint oil on mice, and how long does it last?

People use it in three main ways, and no source cited here says how long the smell stays strong enough to matter. The advice you find online involves soaking cotton balls with the oil, mixing it into a spray, or buying a ready-made pouch, granule or spray product sold for the job.

If you buy a ready-made product, follow the directions on its label rather than a recipe from somewhere else. A bottle sold as an essential oil for other uses is unlikely to carry directions for mice. That leaves a homemade mixture with no tested concentration, no stated schedule and no label precautions. Nothing cited on this page gives a concentration, amount or schedule shown to repel mice.

Duration is the biggest unknown. A scent is something that evaporates, so it is reasonable to expect it to weaken over time, and none of the sources cited here says whether a smell a person can still notice is strong enough to matter to a mouse. If you use a labeled product, follow any replacement interval on its label instead of waiting until you can no longer smell it.
Will mice get used to the smell of peppermint oil?

They might, but that is an expectation drawn from related evidence, not a result measured for peppermint. The nearest evidence is about sound. UC IPM says mice quickly become accustomed to regularly repeated sounds, and that there is little evidence that sound, magnetic or vibrational devices of any kind will drive established house mice or rats from buildings. Whether a constant smell stops registering as a threat the way a repeated noise does is a fair question, and the sources cited here do not answer it for peppermint. The same limits hold for sound devices, which are covered in [the evidence on ultrasonic pest repellers](/blog/ultrasonic-pest-repellers-do-they-work).

Several facts about mice make a constant smell a weak tool even if they never get used to it. UC IPM says house mice seldom venture more than 30 feet from their nest sites and food supply, so a mouse in your house is already living close to what it needs. It also reports that house mice removed from their home range by as much as half a mile can find their way back to the nest site, a sign of how strongly they are tied to a place. And CDC says a mouse can fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch (6 mm), so a scent at one gap leaves every other gap open.

What follows is reasoning, not a finding. A mouse deciding whether to cross a scented patch is weighing the smell against what lies on the other side. If the other side is a nest, a food supply and a short walk home, the smell has to be strong to win that argument, and it has to stay strong. Sealing changes the decision for good because it removes the option.
Is peppermint oil safe for cats, dogs and other pets?

It can be harmful, and peppermint oil is named on an animal poison control center's list of essential oils known to cause poisoning in cats. [Pet Poison Helpline's page on essential oils and cats](https://www.petpoisonhelpline.com/blog/essential-oils-cats/) lists peppermint oil alongside wintergreen, pine, cinnamon, clove, eucalyptus and tea tree oils, among others. It says cats lack an essential liver enzyme and so have difficulty metabolizing and eliminating toxins such as essential oils, that the oils are rapidly absorbed both by mouth and across the skin, and that the higher the concentration of the oil, the greater the risk to the cat. It also says concentrated essential oils should never be applied directly to cats.

[Pet Poison Helpline's general page on essential oils](https://www.petpoisonhelpline.com/pet-safety-tips/essential-oils/) says essential oil poisoning can affect all species, with cats and birds at the greatest risk. That page does not name peppermint oil. The most common signs it lists are drooling, vomiting, lethargy, loss of appetite, and irritation of the respiratory tract, skin and mucous membranes. Signs usually develop within 6 to 8 hours with most essential oils, according to the page. Mild cases resolve within a few hours, and severe ones can take 3 to 7 days to resolve fully.

The same page ranks swallowing as the highest-risk route, then skin contact, then breathing the vapor, and its decontamination advice depends on the route: bathing with liquid dishwashing detergent after skin exposure, early dilution with water or food after swallowing, and fresh air after inhalation. It warns against inducing vomiting because of the risk of aspiration, which means breathing vomit into the lungs. It says an animal with a minor exposure and no signs can be watched closely at home but should go to a veterinarian if signs develop, and it lists a 24-hour line at (855) 764-7661.

For a cat that develops a watery nose or eyes, drooling, vomiting or trouble breathing after inhaling a strong fragrance, the cats page says to move it into fresh air immediately and to get emergency veterinary treatment if the signs do not quickly resolve.

body.title: Cats and mice often share a home
body.text: If a cat, dog or bird lives in the house, keep any scent product, soaked cotton and open bottle out of reach, never put a concentrated oil on a cat, and ask a veterinarian before using one. If a pet may have swallowed, been coated in or breathed in a concentrated oil, call a veterinarian or a pet poison helpline for advice rather than waiting for signs. Pet Poison Helpline says essential oils can affect all species, so ask about other pets such as rabbits, guinea pigs and reptiles too.

The same caution applies to people. If a child swallows a scent product or anyone has a reaction to one, contact a healthcare provider or a poison control center, and keep the label with you so you can read out the ingredients.
Where does peppermint oil fit in a real mouse control plan?

At most as a small add-on after the holes are sealed and the food is secured. It cannot replace sealing, sanitation or trapping, which are the steps the CDC and UC IPM guidance is built on. UC IPM says traps and rodenticides must be combined with preventive measures: sanitation to remove food, water and shelter, and exclusion to keep mice from getting into and moving around a building.

body.text: Sealing is the step the evidence supports

Start by closing the ways in. CDC's page says mice can fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch (6 mm). It advises filling small holes with steel wool, with caulk around it to keep it in place, or using spray foam, and fixing larger holes with lath screen or metal, cement, hardware cloth or metal sheeting. It also mentions flashing around the base of the house. UC IPM adds that house mice can squeeze under gaps 1/4 inch tall and through openings 3/8 inch wide, and that they can jump up to 12 inches from the floor onto a flat surface.

body.needed: Photo of a 1/4 inch gap where a pipe passes through the back of a kitchen cabinet, with a pencil held across the opening for scale, and a second photo of the same gap packed with steel wool and sealed with caulk

body.text: The same CDC page names the places to check:

items: **Inside.** Kitchen cabinets, closets, fireplaces, windows and doors, the space behind appliances, pipes under sinks, vents, and electrical, water and gas lines.
**Outside.** Roof rafters, the gap where the foundation meets the ground, attic vents and holes around utility lines.

body.text: How to pack steel wool and lock it in place is covered in [the guide to steel wool for mice](/blog/steel-wool-for-mice), and [how high and how far mice can climb and jump](/blog/can-mice-climb-walls) explains why upper floors and attics belong on the inspection list.
Trapping, cleanup and when to call a professional

Once the entry points are closed, mice already inside have to be removed. [The guide to mouse traps](/blog/mice-traps) compares the types and explains placement, and the mouse control reference linked above covers safe cleanup of droppings and nests. If you find a nest, keep hearing activity after sealing and trapping, or cannot work out how mice are getting in, [the guide to hiring a mouse exterminator](/blog/mice-exterminator) explains what a professional does and when one is worth it. Comparisons of traps and other tools are collected in [the rodent control product guides](/pest-product-guides/rodent-control).
If you still want to try a scent

items: Finish sealing, secure the food and set up traps first, because those are the steps the sources support.
Choose a product whose label names mice, read the label for ingredients and directions, and follow the label rather than a recipe.
Keep it out of reach of pets and children, and ask a veterinarian first if a cat or bird lives in the home.
Watch for droppings, gnawing and noises. If signs continue, treat that as the scent not working and rely on sealing and trapping.

body.text: Mothballs are not a stronger version of the same idea. They come with legal and health questions of their own, which [the guide to whether mothballs keep mice away](/blog/do-mothballs-keep-mice-away) works through.
Does peppermint oil work in cars, garages and sheds?

The research cited on this page does not separate out vehicles, garages or sheds, so nothing here suggests peppermint oil behaves differently there. The same gaps apply: no measured dose, no stated duration and inconsistent success across study settings. Cars are a common place people try it. [A comparison of tape, strobe lights, peppermint and traps for vehicles](/blog/best-rodent-repellent-for-cars-canada) and [advice on keeping mice out of a car](/blog/how-to-keep-mice-out-of-your-car) cover that setting, including the engine bay and wiring that mice target.

faqs.question: How much peppermint oil do you need to repel mice?
faqs.answer: No source cited on this page gives an amount, a concentration or a schedule that has been shown to repel mice from a home. The 2016 review of plant compounds found inconsistent success across laboratory, enclosure and field studies, so a dose that changes behavior in a cage may not carry over to a house. If you use a ready-made product, its label lists the ingredients, and any directions on that label are the ones to follow.

faqs.question: Does peppermint oil kill mice?
faqs.answer: Nothing cited on this page says peppermint oil kills mice. The claim made for it is that the smell repels them, and the research on that claim is mixed. Traps remove mice and sealing keeps new ones out, while a scent does neither on its own. If mice are already inside, closing the entry points and trapping are the steps the University of California guidance relies on, and CDC's sealing guidance covers the entry points.

faqs.question: Will peppermint oil get mice out of the walls or attic?
faqs.answer: Probably not on its own. UC IPM reports little evidence that sound, magnetic or vibrational devices drive established mice out of buildings, and the 2016 review of plant compounds found inconsistent success across laboratory, enclosure and field studies. House mice seldom venture more than 30 feet from their nest sites and food supply, according to UC IPM, and CDC says they fit through a hole as wide as a pencil. Finding and sealing the entry points is the step the sources support.

faqs.question: Is peppermint oil safe to use around cats?
faqs.answer: It carries a known risk. Pet Poison Helpline lists peppermint oil among the essential oils known to cause poisoning in cats, and says cats and birds are at the greatest risk from essential oils. Signs such as drooling, vomiting and lethargy usually develop within 6 to 8 hours with most essential oils. Keep oils, soaked cotton and scent pouches out of reach, never apply a concentrated oil to a cat, and call a veterinarian or Pet Poison Helpline at (855) 764-7661 if a pet may have been exposed.

faqs.question: Is it legal to sell peppermint oil as a mouse repellent?
faqs.answer: Yes, within limits. Peppermint oil is on the list of active ingredients eligible for EPA's minimum-risk exemption, so a product that meets the six conditions does not need to be registered with EPA, though states may require registration under their own laws. The label cannot claim to control rodents carrying specific diseases or imply that a federal agency endorses the product, and EPA does not review exempted products.

faqs.question: What works better than peppermint oil for mice?
faqs.answer: Sealing the building is the step the sources rank highest. UC IPM calls exclusion the most successful and permanent form of house mouse control, and CDC says mice fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch, and lists materials such as steel wool, caulk, hardware cloth and metal sheeting for closing holes. Pair sealing with removing food and water and with trapping mice already inside.
